result: Conditional knockout of Gng13 in ChAT-expressing tuft cells reduced the number of ectopic tuft cells in injured lungs following H1N1 infection. At 14 dpi, tuft cell densities were similar between WT and Gng13-cKO mice, but at 20, 25, and 50 dpi, WT mice had significantly higher tuft cell densities than Gng13-cKO mice. About 28.6% of tuft cells in WT expressed Gγ13, while none in Gng13-cKO did, confirming effective knockout.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge that the study demonstrates 'a decrease in the overall number of ectopic tuft cells' in Gng13-cKO mice and that the authors 'carefully analyzed phenotypes in mice lacking Gγ13.' The data showing reduced tuft cell numbers at later time points is accepted as solid evidence.

result: Gng13-cKO mice exhibited significantly worse outcomes following H1N1 infection compared to WT mice, including larger areas of lung injury, greater bodyweight loss (30% vs 20% maximum), shifted timing of maximum weight loss, increased mortality (37.5%), and greater wet-to-dry lung mass ratios at 25 dpi.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state that 'support for Gng13 helping to limit influenza injury in the transgenic mouse models used here is solid' and note 'increased lung damage' in Gng13-cKO mice. The thorough assessment of lung injury via multiple techniques is acknowledged as a strength.

result: Gng13-cKO mice showed significantly increased macrophage infiltration in injured lung areas at both 20 and 25 dpi compared to WT mice, although both genotypes showed a trend toward inflammation resolution with reduced immune cell numbers from 20 to 25 dpi.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge 'heightened macrophage infiltration when exposed to the H1N1 virus' and note that the study demonstrates 'increased lung damage and heightened macrophage infiltration.' This finding is treated as part of the solid evidence for Gng13's role in limiting injury.

result: Gng13-cKO mice exhibited augmented pyroptosis and cell death following H1N1 infection, with significantly higher expression of pyroptosis pathway genes and proteins (Gsdmd, Gsdme, NLRP3, Casp1, IL-1β) at 25 dpi compared to WT. The majority of Gsdmd+ and Gsdme+ cells were F4/80+ macrophages, and more than half of CD64+ macrophages were Sytox+, indicating active pyroptosis.
evaluation: Reviewers note that the study's findings include 'greater inflammation' and acknowledge the thorough assessment of lung injury. The pyroptosis data is part of the comprehensive phenotypic analysis that reviewers consider solid evidence for Gng13's protective role.

result: Gng13-cKO mice exhibited severer pulmonary epithelial leakage following H1N1 infection, as evidenced by significantly increased BALF cell numbers, protein content, LDH activity, and IL-1β levels at 20 and 25 dpi compared to WT mice. Notably, IL-1β levels in Gng13-cKO did not decrease from 20 to 25 dpi, unlike other markers.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge that the study demonstrates worsened 'lung inflammation resolution, epithelial barrier and fibrosis' in Gγ13 null mutants. The BALF analysis is part of the comprehensive assessment that reviewers consider solid evidence.

result: Gng13-cKO mice exhibited worsened fibrosis following H1N1 infection, with significantly higher expression of fibrosis-related genes (Col1a1, Fn1, Timp1) and greater percentages of fibrotic areas at 25 dpi (26.3% vs 12.3% in WT). At 50 dpi, fibrosis remained elevated in Gng13-cKO compared to WT, indicating slower resolution.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly note that 'lung inflammation resolution, epithelial barrier and fibrosis were worsen in Gγ13 null mutants.' The fibrosis data is accepted as part of the solid evidence for worse outcomes in Gng13-cKO mice.

result: Trpm5-/- mice showed similar bodyweight loss/recovery curves and tuft cell densities as WT mice following H1N1 infection, with nearly no mortality. This contrasts with the severe phenotype in Gng13-cKO mice, indicating that Trpm5 is not required for ectopic tuft cell proliferation or protection against H1N1 injury.
evaluation: Reviewers note this finding 'was in stark contrast to deletion of Trpm5' and express confusion about the discrepancy. One reviewer states 'the central discrepancy between the lack of a phenotype in Pou2f3 and Trpm5 KO mice compared to the stronger phenotype in the Chat-Cre / Gng13 KO mice remains unresolved.' This indicates uncertainty about the interpretation.

result: The authors conclude that the Gγ13-mediated signal transduction pathway is critical for tuft cell-mediated inflammation resolution and functional repair, proposing that Gγ13-positive and Gγ13-negative tuft cell subsets play opposite but balanced roles. They hypothesize that Gγ13+ tuft cells promote resolution by producing anti-inflammatory mediators, while remaining Gγ13- tuft cells may contribute to prolonged inflammation.
evaluation: Reviewers note that 'evidence for these effects being mediated by normal tuft cells remains incomplete' and that the authors 'speculate that heterogeneity within nascent tuft cell populations, specifically the presence of pro- and anti-inflammatory tuft cells, may explain this difference, but they do not provide any data to support this idea.' One reviewer states the model 'remains unresolved and will require future work.'

result: The authors note a striking discrepancy between their findings and prior reports showing that Pou2f3 knockout (which eliminates all tuft cells) did not significantly affect H1N1 pathogenesis, while their Gng13 conditional knockout (which reduces only a subset of tuft cells) worsened outcomes. They speculate this may be due to imbalance of tuft cell functions.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly identify this as a major weakness, stating the findings are 'at odds with reports from other groups demonstrating no obvious phenotype upon influenza infection in mice lacking the transcription factor Pou2f3.' One reviewer notes 'the central discrepancy... remains unresolved' and another states this creates 'conflicting data from mice that lack tuft cells entirely.'

result: Specific Tas2r bitter taste receptors (Tas2r105, Tas2r108, Tas2r118, Tas2r137, Tas2r138) were upregulated in H1N1-infected lungs at 25 dpi. Subsets of ectopic tuft cells responded functionally to bitter compounds (denatonium benzoate, quinine) with calcium increases, and these responses were completely inhibited by AITC, gallein, or U73122, indicating functional Tas2r signaling.
evaluation: Reviewers do not specifically critique these findings, and they are presented as supporting evidence for tuft cell heterogeneity and function. The calcium imaging data demonstrating functional responses is part of the thorough characterization that reviewers acknowledge.

result: Ectopic tuft cells can be formed in the distal lung following H1N1 infection, appearing around 12-14 days post-infection. H1N1-infected mice showed bodyweight loss peaking at 8-9 dpi with massive alveolar damage, epithelial dysplasia, and increased CD45+ immune cells. About 78% of ChAT-expressing cells in injured lungs also expressed the tuft cell marker Dclk1.
evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these basic characterization findings. The timing and characterization of ectopic tuft cell formation is accepted as background context for the main findings about Gng13's role.

result: Reanalysis of published single-cell RNAseq data showed that about 57% of Trpm5-GFP+ tuft cells were Gγ13+ in WT mice, and some of these also expressed Alox5, a key enzyme for biosynthesis of pro-resolving mediators. Pulmonary ectopic tuft cells express genes encoding enzymes producing specialized pro-resolving mediators (SPMs).
evaluation: Reviewers do not specifically critique this reanalysis of published data. It is presented as supporting evidence for the hypothesis about tuft cell heterogeneity and function, though reviewers note the overall model remains uncertain.

result: Background claims about tuft cells: they are rare epithelial cells expressing chemosensory signaling proteins (Tas1r3, Tas2rs, Vmn2r26, α-gustducin, Gβγ13, Trpm5) that detect pathogens and release signaling molecules (IL-25, prostaglandins, leukotrienes, acetylcholine). Tuft cells are heterogeneous and normally found in nasal cavity and trachea, rarely distal to lung hilus.
evaluation: These are established background facts supported by citations. Reviewers do not challenge these foundational claims about tuft cell biology.
